content: Thuja occidentalis, commonly known as the white cedar tree, is an evergreen coniferous tree belonging to the cypress family, Cupressaceae. It is native to the northeastern United States and southeastern Canada but is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant. The natural distribution of Thuja occidentalis spans from Manitoba eastward through the Great Lakes region and into Québec, Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia. Isolated populations are also found further south in states such as Massachusetts, Connecticut, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, and West Virginia. The species was first described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753, and its binomial name remains unchanged. It is known by various common names, including white cedar (in the UK), yellow cedar, Atlantic white cedar, swamp cedar, Eastern white cedar, false white cedar, hackmatack, and arborvitae. The name arborvitae, meaning tree of life in Latin, reflects its historical medicinal uses, particularly the sap, bark, and twigs. Despite its common names, it is not a true cedar and is unrelated to the Australian white cedar (Melia azedarach). Ecologically, Thuja occidentalis thrives in wet forests, particularly in coniferous swamps where larger, faster-growing trees cannot compete. It also grows in areas with reduced competition, such as cliffs. While not currently listed as endangered, wild populations face threats in many regions due to high deer populations. Deer are particularly attracted to the soft evergreen foliage, which they consume rapidly during winter. The largest known specimen of this tree is 34 meters tall with a diameter of 175 cm, located on South Manitou Island in Michigan. In certain conditions, the tree can live for an exceptionally long time. Notably, some specimens growing on cliffs, where they are protected from deer and wildfires, have been found to be over 1,100 years old. A dead specimen with over 1,650 growth rings has also been discovered. These ancient trees, despite their age, are often small and stunted due to the challenging growing conditions. One famous example, the Witch Tree on Lake Superior in Minnesota, was described as a mature tree in 1731 and remains alive today. Specimens on cliff faces in southern Ontario are among the oldest trees in Eastern North America and Canada, with ages exceeding 1,653 years. Thuja occidentalis holds significant cultural and practical importance, particularly in traditional Ojibwe culture, where it is honored as Nookomis Giizhik or Grandmother Cedar. It is considered a sacred gift to humanity and is used in crafts, construction, and medicine. It is one of the four plants of the Ojibwe medicine wheel, associated with the south. The foliage is rich in vitamin C and is believed to have cured scurvy in Jacques Cartier's expedition during the winter of 1535–1536. However, internal use of the plant can be harmful due to the presence of the neurotoxic compound thujone, especially if used for prolonged periods or during pregnancy. Commercially, northern white cedar is used for rustic fencing, posts, lumber, poles, shingles, and log cabin construction. It is the preferred wood for structural elements like ribs and planking in birchbark canoes and wooden canoes. The essential oil derived from the plant has been utilized in cleansers, disinfectants, hair preparations, insecticides, liniments, room sprays, and soft soaps. Historically, the Ojibwe made soup from the inner bark of the soft twigs, and others have used the twigs to make teas for relieving constipation and headaches. In the 19th century, Thuja was commonly used as an externally applied tincture or ointment for treating warts, ringworm, and thrush. Injecting the tincture into venereal warts was reported to cause their disappearance. Thuja occidentalis is widely cultivated as an ornamental tree, particularly for screens and hedges in gardens, parks, and cemeteries. Popular cultivars include 'Emerald Green,' 'Techny,' and 'Wareana.' The tree was introduced to Europe as early as 1540.
